title: Mining stocks: how to analyze mining companies
description: Mining stocks: ore grade arithmetic, the leverage of the C1 cost ladder and the slow supply cycle — how to read a mining company's economics.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
# Mining stocks: how to analyze mining companies

**Mining stocks are shares in companies whose product is an element blasted, crushed and smelted out of rock.** The product cannot be differentiated or renewed; the remaining edge is the rock: ore grade, cost ladder, the cycle's patience. The sector becomes the market's purest cost-and-cycle laboratory; the analysis, arithmetic. The [mining and metals sector course](/kurser/se-20-gruv-och-metallsektorn) gathers them; AK1A's company universe spans iron ore, copper, gold and diversified metals: Vale, Freeport-McMoRan, Fortescue, Northern Star, South32 — and Sweden's Boliden. Here is the analysis, with the universe's numbers.

## Ore grade — the mining stocks' moat in the rock

The mine's most fundamental number is the metal share in the rock: ore grade decides tons of rock per ton of finished metal. Course example: a deposit at 1.0 percent copper requires 100 tons of rock per ton of copper; at 40 dollars per ton of rock, mining and processing land at 4,000 dollars per ton. The neighbor at 2.0 percent moves 50 tons, lands at 2,000 dollars — half the grade, double the cost. No management negotiates with geology: process knowledge can be copied, cost curves optimized — the rock's copper share holds no meeting. Grade development is the mining version of [moat erosion](/kurser/mt-01-vad-ar-en-moat): richest ore first, so the average grade declines over the mine's life — a built-in cost headwind, rarely in the annual report, always in the life-of-mine plan.

## Cash margin — the C1 ladder and leverage

The sector's central earnings measure is the cash margin: price per pound minus cash cost C1, per pound of finished metal, net of credits. Two examples at the same price, 4.00 dollars per pound: the northern mine, C1 1.60, margin 2.40 dollars; the high-mountain mine, C1 2.80, margin 1.20. Leverage is price divided by price minus C1 — 1.67 versus 3.33. A ten percent move up, to 4.40, gives margins of 2.80 and 1.60: plus 16.7 and plus 33.3 percent. The mirror down, to 3.60, gives 2.00 and 0.80 — same property, two directions: largest upside in the boom, fastest suffocation at bottom. The zero points — 1.60 versus 2.80 — are the cycle bottom's sorting mechanism: when the price passes a mine's C1 it is idled, step by step up the ladder. The fuller measure AISC always sits above C1; read both — C1 for today's cash machine, AISC for how long it lasts. The cost position is the [cost leadership unit](/kurser/mt-06-kostnadsoverlagsenhet) in its most extreme condition.

## Five metals, five cycles — what the commodity does to the accounts

The universe's mining family is not one group but distinct commodity cycles. Vale, the world's largest iron ore and pellet producer, saw gross margin fall from 60.0 percent in 2021 to 35.0 in 2025 as the price turned; net income fell 47.6 percent per year 2022–2025. Fortescue, the Pilbara iron ore miner, rode the same roller coaster: gross margin 56.0 to 40.1 percent — minus 15.9 units — dividends 6,699 to 2,529 million dollars, minus 62 percent from peak. A mining cycle's dividend follows earnings, not policy. Freeport-McMoRan, the largest listed pure-play copper producer with Grasberg among the world's largest deposits, swung softer: gross margin 42.6 to 37.1 percent 2022–2025. Copper is the metal of electrification, and every new mine takes decades — supply answers slowly to structural demand. Northern Star shows the opposite cycle: gold lifted gross margin from 14.3 to 37.8 percent — plus 23.4 units — while iron ore fell. Same country, same sector, opposite cycles. South32, BHP's 2015 spin-off with aluminum, manganese and nickel, took two loss years (minus 173 and minus 203 million dollars) on impairments of 1,300 and 604, then turned to 1,087 million profit. Sweden's Boliden, covered by the [case course](/kurser/pc-11-case-boliden): revenue grew from 86,437 to 93,509 million kronor 2022–2025 — plus 8.2 percent — earnings fell from 12,410 to 9,404 million, minus 24.2. The price turns, the volume carries — the margin decides.

## Supply inertia — the cycle answers out of phase

From discovery to production takes five to ten years: exploration, permits, mine and concentrator construction. The course's history-shaped example: a demand shock (the China construction boom of the 2000s) doubles the price from 2.00 to 4.00 dollars per pound over six years — plus 100 percent — while world production grows eight percent. Four years later the tonnage lands, demand has turned, and the price falls 45 percent to 2.20. The market side — prices, bids, the materials branch's median profiles — is owned by the [commodity cycle guide](/blogg/ravarubolag-materialbranschens-cykel); the mining side's consequence is reading. One year's earnings reflect that year's price — [normalized multiples](/kurser/vr-02-normaliserade-multipler) are a necessity, not a nicety. The largest investment programs sit near the price peak, where financing is best — the investment peak is itself a [business cycle indicator](/kurser/ma-04-konjunkturindikatorerna) reading in reverse: the most is built when most dangerous.

## By-products and reserves — what each ton is worth

Sulfide ores are rarely pure: the copper rock carries gold, silver, zinc and lead, separated into products. Course example per ton of ore: a copper grade of 1.2 percent yields twelve kilos of metal worth around 106 dollars; the gold credit — 0.5 grams at 65 dollars the gram — adds 33 dollars. Of the 139 dollars of revenue per ton, the gold carries almost a quarter. The credit works in two places: in revenue as gold cash, in cost — C1 is calculated net of credits. Two mines with identical C1 can differ if one's C1 is carried by a gold credit; Grasberg carries a significant gold by-product — copper and gold, two legs of one mountain. Reserves set the time axis: 6.0 million tons of metal at 0.2 million tons annual production gives a 30-year life. Price and technology move the reservation — a reserve increase can be a price statement, not a discovery — and a mine lives three to five price cycles. Valued at a cycle peak, an asset's first decade may be its worst.

## Capital cycle and minority interests — the report's two special items

Two items separate mining reports from others'. First, the capital program. Freeport's investments rose from 3,469 to 4,494 million dollars 2022–2025; free cash flow swung between 1,670, 455, 2,352 and 1,116 million — smelter years ate cash, the recovery year gave it back. Northern Star built five years straight above one billion Australian dollars, 1,061 to 2,713 million, while free cash flow landed at 471 million against net income 1,664: profit exists, cash builds a mine. Read the [balance sheet](/kurser/bk-01-balansrakningen) before the income statement. Second, minority interests: Freeport books all of Grasberg in consolidation but carries 48.8 percent economic interest; of total equity of 32.2 billion dollars, 12.1 billion is minority interest — 38 percent. Finally, land: a deposit's jurisdictions are a [regulatory risk](/kurser/rk-06-regulatorisk-risk) — in Sweden, Bergsstaten at [SGU](https://www.sgu.se/bergsstaten) tries processing concessions; permit length is part of the supply inertia.

## Valuation: the multiple against the cycle

Cycle earnings turn P/E into a bottom trick. Vale's P/E of 30.72 reflects cycle-bottom earnings — the same company is valued at 8.71 on next year's forecast; Fortescue trades at 12.43, free cash flow yield 10.3 percent. A low P/E on peak earnings, a high on trough earnings — one phenomenon, two mirrors: E is a price cycle. Compare mining stocks within the family, against the [sector medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2), with the [sector analysis method](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod) — revenue engine, margin engine, balance — and the [P/E course](/kurser/km-009-pe) warnings in mind.

## Checklist: six questions when you analyze mining stocks

1. **Ore grade development** — what does the life-of-mine plan say about grade decline?
2. **C1 and AISC** — where in the cost ladder does the mine sit, and what carries C1: own costs or credits?
3. **Cycle position** — where does the price stand against a normalized average, and is the sector at peak investment?
4. **Reserves and mine life** — how many years do the reserves last at today's production rate?
5. **Capital program and minorities** — where is the cash going, and whose earnings are you reading?
6. **Jurisdiction** — which countries, which permits govern the deposits?

Mining stocks reward those who calculate on the rock instead of predicting the price: ore grade owns cost, cost ladder owns the cycle's bottom, supply's slow answer owns the cycle. The whole materials branch is in the [materials sector course](/kurser/km-045-materialsektorn); the complete method in the [complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).
